title: Data Privacy
body:
**Data privacy** is the legal and ethical block, and its first move is separating what is legal
from what people expect. Consent obtained by a document nobody reads is valid in law and close
to meaningless in practice, and most of the debate lives in that gap.

Three distinctions the course insists on:

**Volunteered against inferred.** Data you typed in is one category. Data derived about you
from behaviour is another, and it is frequently more sensitive, since purchase patterns and
timing reveal things nobody would have entered in a form.

**Collection against use.** Agreeing to a service collecting data for one purpose is not
agreement to every later purpose, and a dataset gathered for delivery logistics can be sold,
merged or subpoenaed afterwards.

**Anonymous against de-identified.** Removing names is weaker than it sounds. A small number of
attributes, such as a postcode with a birth date and a sex, identifies most individuals
uniquely, so a de-identified dataset cross-referenced against any other dataset frequently
re-identifies people.

Data collection as a business model is what makes this structural. A service given away free is
paid for by the data it gathers, so the incentive runs toward collecting more than the service
needs, and a privacy-preserving design costs the provider revenue.

[[Social Contract Theory]] supplies the sharpest test, asking whether a rational
person understanding the arrangement would have agreed to it.
[[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] builds the mechanisms, in [[Cookies]] and the
[[Cookie Jar]], and [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] is what makes a privacy guarantee enforceable by
mathematics.
